newsitem.title: USA: Throwing out old blue jeans? Think again.
newsitem.headline: Throwing out old blue jeans? Think again.

text.p: The arrival of autumn means it's time to start digging out warmer clothing, and for some people that will mean tossing out old blue jeans. But doing that could be like throwing away hundred dollar bills.

"People can get $50, $100 or $200 for true vintage items," said Max Shapiro, a clothing dealer from San Francisco, referring to blue jeans and other classic American clothing that's at least 25 years old.
"People are shocked that we'll pay that much."

But Shapiro, and other dealers like him, are willing to fork out the money because they turn around and sell the old jeans, jean jackets and other vintage items to retailers in Europe and Asia, especially Japan, at a hefty profit.
Retailers then sell the stuff to people eager to own a bit of Americana, sometimes at double the prices they paid.

In case you didn't know it, the market for vintage blue jeans is hot. Even jeans that are only 10 or 20 years old can fetch $65 or so, although the loftiest prices are for those at least 25 years old and in good condition.
While most people don't have vintage jeans lying around, those who find old denim pants or jackets boxed in the attic or stashed in a drawer somewhere could be in for a windfall.

Shapiro tells the story of two brothers, both in their 50s, and their father, from a small town in northern California, who together had about 50 vintage jeans and jackets. After hearing about Shapiro and his business, Green for Jeans, on a television show, they contacted him and negotiations started.

Eventually, Shapiro agreed to pay $15,000 for the goods. At closing the men insisted on being paid in cash, and they even asked their banker to call the Federal Reserve to check the authenticity of the bills.

Shapiro said he didn't mind. That find, as well as a more recent one in the South -- a man with about 15 pair of Levi's 501 jeans with the original tags on them, probably 25 years old or more -- are "a vintage clothing dealer's dream."

"If you can find them, they're great," said Marc Luers, owner of Tatters, a clothing retailer and wholesaler in Minneapolis. "They've become scarce and there's an awful lot of people looking for them."
Competition among dealers scrounging for supply is so keen that none interviewed for this article would divulge specific sources, or even the cities where they were looking.
But the dealers regularly scout garage sales, flea markets and thrift stores in small towns and farming communities west of the Mississippi, where most vintage jeans are likely to be found.

The most popular items are blue jeans made by Levi Strauss & Co., which have been a hot American commodity around the world for more than two decades. But old Wrangler and Lee jeans can bring top dollar as well.
The thirst for things American, especially in Japan, is what drives the market.

"Demand for vintage jeans is 98 percent from Japan," Shapiro said. "In Japan, students wear uniforms in school, and since they often don't have big houses or cars, they make statements with the clothing they wear."

New Levi's jeans can cost up to $100 in most developed countries, so people in Japan, Thailand and elsewhere in Asia or Europe are often willing to pay that much or more for older jeans, which are more of a status symbol.
Even used American sneakers have been hot in Japan, with used Air Jordans in good condition fetching up to several hundred dollars, though that trend seems to have cooled.
But vintage jeans and jackets continue rising in price, by as much as 20 percent a year, according to dealers.
If you have old jeans or jackets, here are some things to look for:
-- red lines running up the inseams on the inside of the legs. The most common older Levi 501 jean, the "Redlines" can fetch up to $65 in good condition. Produced until 1986.
-- the letter 'e' on the red tag on the right back pocket. If the 'e' in Levi's is capitalised, you have a so-called Big E that can bring up to $200 in good condition.
-- rivets inside the back pockets. The "Double X" Big E 501 model was produced until 1965 and now fetches about $400.
-- an adjustable belt in back attached by copper rivets. Very rare, these fetch up to $2,000 in good condition.

Levi Strauss & Co. stopped making the buckle-back model in 1942 due to government efforts to save metal and fabric during World War II, according to Kay McDonough, assistant historian at Levi Strauss & Co., which started making jeans in 1873.
Items from other makers can also command good prices.
Authentic Lee cowboy pants in good condition from the 1940s, with a crotch rivet, buckle back and a button that says "Lee Cowboy", could bring $1,000, Shapiro said.
A Wrangler souvenir rodeo jacket with bright yellow embroidery can fetch $700.
To order Shapiro's free handbook, "Taking Your Blue Jeans to the Bank" ($2.95 for postage), call 800 538-4799.
